newsitem.title: USA: Cable modem prices drop, spurring faster links.
newsitem.headline: Cable modem prices drop, spurring faster links.

text.p: Modem manufacturers, led by Zenith Electronics Corp. and Motorola Inc., have cut prices on cable modems, putting the high-speed connections within reach of many home computer users.

The impact of the price cuts was seen Tuesday when Time Warner Inc. agreed to buy 250,000 cable modems from Motorola, one day after Zenith said it cut the price of its cable modems to $299 for orders of 1,000 or more.
Analysts said the expense of the modems was the main factor preventing widespread use of the technology and the $300 barrier was seen as a key level.

"This is encouraging," said Rakesh Sood, an analyst with investment banker Hambrecht & Quist. "I think it's another milestone along the way to cable modems becoming more pervasive, but I think we're still some months if not quarters away from having widespread deployment."
Zenith said on Monday it will offer its cable modems for $299 when purchased in quantities of 1,000 or more. In smaller quantities, the price is now $399, down from $495 previously.

"It's an indication that they are making progress on lowering the price of the modem, which has been one of the hindrances of widespread adoption in the marketplace," said Peter Andrew at brokers A.G. Edwards & Sons.

Cable modems allow computer connections to the Internet and other networks over cable television cable rather than thin telephone lines. Connection speeds are hundreds of times faster than with conventional telephone modems.
Time Warner, the second largest U.S. cable TV operator, offers its Road Runner online service in a few cities and plans to launch the service in 10 additional markets in 1997.
Motorola's cable modem would allow a user to send and receive information at speeds far greater that the fastest analog telephone line modems.
"The extraordinary market demand for cable modems has enabled us to drop the price significantly for this order," said John Battin, senior vice president of Motorola's Multimedia Group.
The Motorola/Time Warner deal is valued at about $75 million.
Robert Wilkes, an analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman, said the price cut is another sign that 1997 will be the year the cable modem will take off.
"I've thought that's going to be the case and these price reductions make it more likely that it's going to happen," Wilkes said.
In cable Internet connection services, cable companies have provided the modems to their subscribers. This is similar to providing set-top boxes as part of the monthly fee for cable television.

"It's very important for the cable industry to get cable modem pricing down if they're going to offer subscribers an affordable service and at the same time recoup the price of the modem," Wilkes said, adding that the modems typically had been priced at $400 to $500.
Wilkes said he expected companies to begin shipping the modems in volume in the second half of 1997, and more and more cable companies to offer the service on a widespread basis.
U.S. Robotics Corp., the world's top supplier of desktop modems, has said it will also supply cable modems, as well as the systems cable operators need to provide Internet access.
The company, however, has said it plans to target consumers rather than cable companies.
But even with lower prices, many analysts were cautious.

Most cable operators need to make costly and time-consuming upgrades to their systems to make them "two-way." Cable television is broadcast from one point to many, whereas an Internet connection requires a two-way, interactive system.
